articles.title: AVIF Explained: Smaller Images, Same Quality — Should You Switch?
articles.excerpt: Images are usually the heaviest part of any web page, and the format you choose decides how heavy. AVIF is the newest image format on the block, built on the AV1 video codec — and for photos it produc…
articles.body: Images are usually the heaviest part of any web page, and the format you choose decides how heavy. AVIF is the newest image format on the block, built on the AV1 video codec — and for photos it produces noticeably smaller files than JPEG or WebP at the same visual quality. Where AVIF wins Photographs and detailed images. AVIF keeps fine detail and smooth gradients while cutting file size, which means faster page loads and less data for your visitors — especially on mobile connections. All major browsers have supported AVIF for a while now, so the compatibility worry that held it back is mostly gone. Where it doesn't (yet) Simple graphics: for logos, icons, and illustrations, SVG is still the right tool — it's resolution-independent and usually lighter.

articles.body: Hardening Tool-Call Accuracy in vLLM: Deterministic Agent Execution at Scale Self-hosting open-weights Large Language Models for autonomous multi-agent workloads is often heralded as the ultimate path toward data sovereignty and predictable latency. However, production engineers repeatedly encounter a brutal failure mode: tool-call degradation . While proprietary endpoints (such as OpenAI's GPT-4o or Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet) handle tool definitions and invocation schemas behind opaque, heavily engineered orchestration layers, self-hosting via vLLM exposes raw tokenization friction. A recent deep-dive by Ubicloud tackled these regressions directly. Here is an architectural teardown of why tool calling breaks in vLLM and how to enforce deterministic execution in production. 1.

articles.title: Integrating an AI Assistant into an Existing Application
articles.excerpt: Adding an AI assistant to an existing application is not primarily a chat-interface problem. It is an application architecture problem. The interface may be a small panel or a conversational screen, b…
articles.body: Adding an AI assistant to an existing application is not primarily a chat-interface problem. It is an application architecture problem. The interface may be a small panel or a conversational screen, but the assistant still needs to authenticate users, retrieve the right information, respect existing permissions, call approved tools and fail safely when it cannot complete a task. This tutorial walks through a practical architecture for integrating a large language model (LLM) into an existing web application. It covers authentication, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), tool permissions, logging, evaluation, privacy and human handoff. The examples are architectural illustrations, not a complete, production-ready implementation.

articles.title: Agents that survive real use: verify, never submit blind, and log everything
articles.excerpt: I build agents that act in the real world: a WhatsApp bot with dozens of commands, and an app with server-verified missions. The interesting part is not the model. It is everything around it that keep…
articles.body: I build agents that act in the real world: a WhatsApp bot with dozens of commands, and an app with server-verified missions. The interesting part is not the model. It is everything around it that keeps the agent from doing damage when it is wrong. These are the rules I actually work by, learned the hard way. 1. Never submit blind An agent must never send, commit, push, or publish something I have not seen, unless I explicitly ordered that exact action. Drafts go to a staging area first. Live code is only touched after a check passes in a throwaway copy. This rule exists because of a real incident: a bot command once committed and pushed a change without my approval. The change stayed, but the rule changed with it. No agent query touches live code or a live repo on its own. 2.

articles.title: I shipped a real app on a GitHub JSON backend, and it works until it doesn't
articles.excerpt: I needed a backend for a small discovery feed app. No database was provisionable at the time, and I did not want to pay for one before the app had any users. So I used what I already had: a private Gi…
articles.body: I needed a backend for a small discovery feed app. No database was provisionable at the time, and I did not want to pay for one before the app had any users. So I used what I already had: a private GitHub repo, a JSON file in it, and Vercel serverless functions. This is not a recommendation for every app. It is a record of what worked, what broke, and where it stops working. The shape The app is a feed of events, offers, and stores. Viewers are read-only. Only an admin can post, edit, delete, or hide a post. There are no accounts and no payments yet. The data lives in one file, data/kairo.json , in a private repo. Nothing reads or writes that file from the browser. Every read and write goes through a serverless function, and only the server holds the token that can write to the repo.

articles.title: Rubin telescope should find more of Earth's mysterious 'mini-moons' — including some we can study up close
articles.excerpt: Earth’s tiny, temporary moons could become some of the easiest asteroid targets for future missions. And we'll likely find more of them soon, thanks to the Rubin telescope.
articles.body: Earth almost always has more than one moon. The others are just very small, and they never stay long — but they could provide accessible and unique insights into the solar system. Temporary satellites, or mini-moons , are small asteroids that wander into Earth’s neighborhood and get captured briefly by our planet’s gravity. A typical one stays about nine months and circles Earth roughly three times before escaping back into orbit around the sun , Grigori Fedorets of Finland's University of Helsinki said in a presentation at the Europlanet Science Congress (EPSC) 2026 in The Hague in September. Fedorets' modeling suggests that the largest mini-moon around Earth at any given moment is typically only about 75 centimeters (30 inches) across.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. M42: The Great Nebula in Orion Explanation: The Great Nebula in Orion , an immense, nearby starbirth region , is one the most famous of all astronomical nebulas . Here, glowing gas surrounds hot young stars at the edge of an immense interstellar molecular cloud only 1500 light-years away. In the featured deep image in assigned colors highlighted by emission in hydrogen , wisps and sheets of dust and gas are particularly evident.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.
